entities.name: Jijeung of Silla
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Jijeung of Silla (437–514 CE) stands as the 22nd ruler and the inaugural monarch of the Koreanic kingdom of Silla, reigning from 500 to 514 CE. His 14-year reign marked a pivotal transition for Silla, transforming it from a loosely organized tribal confederacy into a centralized, expansionist kingdom. He is historically significant for institutionalizing royal authority, establishing foundational administrative frameworks, and initiating the territorial consolidation that would later enable Silla's unification of the Korean Peninsula.

During his rule, Jijeung implemented a series of transformative reforms. In 503 CE, he formally adopted the title of "King" (Wang, 왕), replacing the earlier, less authoritative "Maripgan" and thereby consolidating the monarch's power and legitimizing Silla as a sovereign state. He standardized the measurement system and significantly boosted agricultural productivity by introducing oxen for plowing, a technological advancement with profound economic implications. Militarily, his most notable achievement was the conquest of Usan-guk (modern-day Ulleungdo and Dokdo islands) in 512 CE, expanding Silla's maritime domain and securing vital coastal trade routes. He also established Ushi-san Guk as the kingdom's first administrative division (gun) in 505 CE, signaling an emerging bureaucratic structure.

Jijeung's reforms had profound and lasting consequences, fundamentally reshaping Silla's internal structure and external projection. By centralizing royal power and establishing a more robust administrative and territorial apparatus, he created the necessary conditions for his successors, particularly Beopheung and Jinheung, to pursue aggressive expansion, implement Buddhist statecraft, and achieve cultural assimilation. His reign solidified Silla's identity as a distinct and formidable state, setting the stage for its eventual emergence as the dominant power on the peninsula and paving the way for the Unified Silla period.

His reforms directly led to a stronger state capable of significant expansion.
